PD also includes various formal and informal activities like workshops, courses, coaching, mentoring, conferences, etc. (Parkhouse et al., 2019; Postholm, 2012). The diversity of teacher development programs has led to a body of research aiming to identify the characteristics of highquality PD activities (Blank & de Las Alas, 2009; Desimone, 2009; Kennedy, 2016; Sims & Fletcher-Wood, 2020). Previous research suggests that PD should focus on teacher’s interests, needs, prior knowledge and real-life contexts. Building subject knowledge and pedagogical skills (in contrast to general pedagogical techniques) through active methods can provide meaningful learning experiences which are related to teachers’ daily work in the classroom (Blank & de Las Alas, 2009; Desimone, 2009; Dunst, Bruder, & Hamby, 2015; Patton, Parker, & Tannehill, 2015). Further, knowledge sharing in teacher collaboration activities (professional learning communities, community of practice, learning communities of educators) is beneﬁcial for improving teachers’ practice (Bryk et al., 1999; Doğan & Yurtseven, 2018; Vescio, Ross, & Adams, 2008) and student outcomes (McLaughlin & Talbert, 2006; Patton et al., 2015; Vangrieken et al., 2015; Vescio et al., 2008). Teachers’ participation in PD activities focusing on teacher collaboration and active learning methods are more likely to use these strategies in their teaching (Barrera-Pedemonte, 2016). The complexity of real-life teaching and learning environments has to be considered because teaching and learning is contextually situated (Anderson et al., 2000; Opfer & Pedder, 2011).
